steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Impact" section of a Wikipedia article on the AACS encryption key controversy: how the key spread online after the Digg episode, how the media and others reacted, and how the AACS LA responded.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
After what happened on Digg and the call to "Spread this number", the key was quickly posted to thousands of pages, blogs and wikis across the Internet. The reaction was an example of the Streisand effect.

Intellectual property lawyer Douglas J. Sorocco said, "People are getting creative. It shows the futility of trying to stop this. Once the information is out there, cease-and-desist letters are going to infuriate this community more." Outside of the Internet and the mass media, the key has appeared in or on T-shirts, poetry, songs and music videos, illustrations and other graphic artworks, tattoos and body art, and comic strips. The Linux kernel also had a copy of the key in it for 17.5 years. David Woodhouse originally added it in 2007 as part of the red zone logic and it was then removed in 2024 as a routine cleanup.

On Tuesday afternoon, May 1, 2007, searching Google for the key returned 9,410 results, and the same search the next morning returned nearly 300,000 results. On Friday, the BBC reported that a search on Google showed almost 700,000 pages had published the key, even though on April 17 the AACS LA had sent a DMCA notice to Google demanding that Google stop returning any results for searches for the key.

- widespread news coverage: user-driven websites, legal liability of running one, perception of DRM acceptance, failure of "secrecy based businesses ... in every aspect" in Internet era, harm of harshly-perceived legal action
- Carter Wood, National Association of Manufacturers, removed "Digg It" link from weblog [quote: Carter Wood]
- media at first avoided quoting the key; several US news sources then ran it, quoting Digg; no known DMCA notices; later reports quoted it
- Current TV, Google Current story, May 3, 2007: key on screen several seconds, story on website
- May 1, 2007 Wikipedia lockout "to prevent the former secret from being posted again"; HD DVD page locked against "The Number"; later reversed; no arrests or charges

### AACS LA reaction

- May 7, 2007 statement on website [quotes: removal solely of circumvention tools; no removal of discussion; encouraged by cooperation]
- earlier BBC News: AACS executive, bloggers "crossed the line", "legal and technical tools", "interesting new twist"

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
After what happened on Digg and the call to "Spread this number", the key was quickly posted to thousands of pages, blogs and wikis across the Internet. The reaction was an example of the Streisand effect.

Intellectual property lawyer Douglas J. Sorocco said, "People are getting creative. It shows the futility of trying to stop this. Once the information is out there, cease-and-desist letters are going to infuriate this community more." Outside of the Internet and the mass media, the key has appeared in or on T-shirts, poetry, songs and music videos, illustrations and other graphic artworks, tattoos and body art, and comic strips. The Linux kernel also had a copy of the key in it for 17.5 years. David Woodhouse originally added it in 2007 as part of the red zone logic and it was then removed in 2024 as a routine cleanup.

On Tuesday afternoon, May 1, 2007, searching Google for the key returned 9,410 results, and the same search the next morning returned nearly 300,000 results. On Friday, the BBC reported that a search on Google showed almost 700,000 pages had published the key, even though on April 17 the AACS LA had sent a DMCA notice to Google demanding that Google stop returning any results for searches for the key.

There was widespread news coverage. It included speculation about the development of user-driven websites, the legal liability of running a user-driven website, the perception of acceptance of DRM, the failure as a business model of "secrecy based businesses ... in every aspect" in the Internet era, and the harm that an industry can do to itself with legal action that is perceived as harsh.

In an opposing move, Carter Wood of the National Association of Manufacturers said that they had removed the "Digg It" link from their weblog:

> Until the Digg community shows as much fervor in attacking intellectual piracy as attacking the companies that are legitimately defending their property, well, we do not want to be promoting the site by using the "Digg It" feature.

At first media coverage avoided quoting the key itself. But several US-based news sources have run stories that contain the key, quoting its use on Digg, although none of them are known to have received DMCA notices because of it. Later reports have discussed this, and quoted the key. Current TV broadcast the key during a Google Current story about the Digg incident on May 3, 2007. It displayed the key in full on screen for several seconds and put the story on the station website.

On May 1, 2007, Wikipedia locked out the page named for the number "to prevent the former secret from being posted again". The page on HD DVD was also locked, to keep out "The Number". This was reversed later. No one has been arrested or charged for finding or publishing the original key.

### AACS LA reaction

On May 7, 2007, the AACS LA announced on its website that it had "requested the removal solely of illegal circumvention tools, including encryption keys, from a number of web sites", and that it had "not requested the removal or deletion of any ... discussion or commentary". The statement went on, "AACS LA is encouraged by the cooperation it has received thus far from the numerous web sites that have chosen to address their legal obligations in a responsible manner." Earlier, BBC News had quoted an AACS executive saying that bloggers "crossed the line", that AACS was looking at "legal and technical tools" to confront the people who published the key, and that the events with Digg were an "interesting new twist".
